Bowers v. Hardwick. In June 1986, the Supreme Court ruled five to four that Georgia's anti-sodomy law was constitutional, upholding a state statute that criminalized consensual same-sex conduct between adults, even in private. Justice Byron White wrote the majority opinion, which rejected the claim that the Constitution's right to privacy extends to same-sex relations. White distinguished the case from prior privacy precedents like Roe v. Wade, asserting that none of those prior rulings bore any resemblance to the claimed constitutional right of homosexuals to engage in sodomy. Chief Justice Burger added a concurrence calling homosexuality anathema to centuries of moral teachings. Justice Blackmun's dissent argued the case was ultimately about the fundamental right to be left alone in intimate matters. The decision became widely condemned by LGBTQ advocates and civil rights organizations as a devastating setback. For seventeen years it stood as the law of the land, symbolizing judicial opposition to LGBTQ rights. However, the dissent's reasoning eventually prevailed when Lawrence v. Texas explicitly overturned Bowers and rejected its premises entirely, establishing that the Constitution does protect the dignity and liberty interests of same-sex couples.
